system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell activation syndrome, diffuse esophageal spasm, and coronary artery disease s/p CABG presented with itching, difficulty breathing, and chest tightness during a barium swallow, consistent with a mast cell crisis. She was treated per allergist protocol with IV methylprednisolone, Benadryl, and Dilaudid for pain. Serial troponins were negative and EKG unchanged, ruling out acute cardiac injury. Chest imaging showed low lung volumes without acute findings. The barium swallow revealed esophageal dysmotility and transient hold-up of a pill at the gastroesophageal junction. Her symptoms improved over 36-48 hours. She was discharged home on her baseline medications with follow-up planned with allergist and GI, and recommendations to premedicate with antihistamines for future procedures.
problems: Mast cell neoplasms of uncertain behavior
Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
Presence of right artificial knee joint
Acquired absence of both cervix and uterus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having terrible abdominal pain, especially after eating. And I feel that familiar tightness in my chest again—like my mast cells are flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I see you have a history of mast cell degranulation syndrome and esophageal spasms. Did anything trigger this episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not sure. I didn’t eat anything unusual. But I’ve had this feeling before—itching, flushing, trouble breathing. I knew I’d need Benadryl soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals show your blood pressure is a bit low—87 over 51. We’ll keep an eye on that. You’re also wheezing a little. We’ve started your standard treatment: IV steroids, Benadryl, and some Dilaudid for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That protocol usually helps. But the pain is really sharp—right here in the upper belly. Feels like my esophagus is cramping again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your CT scan of the abdomen came back normal—no gallstones, no appendicitis. So it’s likely related to your known esophageal dysmotility, possibly worsened by the mast cell flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in a few days either. That’s not helping. And my face feels swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That facial swelling and the rash on your chest are common during mast cell activation. We’ll continue monitoring. We’ve given you fluids and will repeat your labs in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I stop my blood pressure meds? I’m on carvedilol and furosemide at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held both for now because your blood pressure has been on the lower side. Once the crisis settles, your regular doctors can reassess if you still need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just don’t want my heart to suffer because we’re focusing on the mast cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Your EKG and three troponin levels are normal, so no sign of heart damage. Your coronary disease is stable. We’re just being cautious with the meds during this episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look better. White count is down, and liver enzymes are improving. We’re planning an EGD today to check your esophagus and possibly inject Botox to help with the spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It helps for a little while, but the spasms always come back. Do you think it’ll make a difference this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may give temporary relief. The goal is to reduce the frequency of spasms, especially since they seem tied to your mast cell symptoms. We’ll do it under sedation, and you’ll be monitored closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust the team. Just please avoid any contrast or dyes—they’ve triggered reactions before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve noted your allergies to iodine, barium, and contrast. No dyes will be used. The procedure is just the scope and Botox injection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the EGD. The procedure went well. They injected Botox at the gastroesophageal junction. No signs of ulcers or strictures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it help with the pain? I still feel tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might take a day or two to see improvement. You did have some relief briefly, but the mast cell symptoms flared again. We gave you another dose of Benadryl and Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so tired of this cycle. It feels like one problem feeds the other.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your allergist and GI team agree they’re linked. That’s why we’re treating both—calming the mast cells helps the spasms, and relaxing the esophagus may reduce triggers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my nausea? I haven’t eaten much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added Zofran for nausea. You can try small sips of clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure is more stable—123 over 72. You’re not wheezing as much, and your rash is fading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. Still some chest tightness, but not as intense. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. We want to make sure you’re stable off IV meds. You’ve switched back to oral Dilaudid and Benadryl, which you’ll continue at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take Benadryl that often forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your allergist will help manage that. For now, we’re giving you diphenhydramine tablets to take by mouth every four hours as needed for tightness or breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my constipation? I still haven’t gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added bisacodyl and senna to help. Stay on the polyethylene glycol too. Hydration and fiber will help once you’re home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll follow up with my GI and allergist. They’re both scheduled next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll send them a summary. In the meantime, keep taking your omeprazole, methadone, and gabapentin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my heart meds? Should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off for now. Your blood pressure is still on the lower side. Your cardiologist should reassess once you’re fully recovered. We’ve noted that in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight—no episodes of low blood pressure or breathing trouble. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s a relief to be going home. Just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve sent prescriptions for diphenhydramine, senna, and bisacodyl. Continue all your other meds except carvedilol and furosemide for now. Call your doctors if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And if I feel a flare coming on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your Benadryl, use your albuterol inhaler, and call your allergist. If you can’t reach them or feel worse, go to the ER. You know your body best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do. Thanks for listening and for not rushing me. I know I’ve been here a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not a burden. We’re here to help you through these flares. Take care, and we hope to see you only in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell degranulation syndrome, achalasia, and coronary artery disease s/p CABG was admitted for abdominal pain and a self-reported mast cell crisis. She presented with epigastric pain worsened by eating, chest tightness, flushing, and wheezing. Treatment followed her allergist’s protocol with IV methylprednisolone, Benadryl, and IV Dilaudid for pain. A CT abdomen showed no acute findings, and troponins remained negative, ruling out cardiac ischemia. She underwent an EGD with Botox injection at the gastroesophageal junction, which provided only transient relief. Her symptoms improved over three days with supportive care. Blood pressure-lowering medications were held due to hypotension during the crisis. She was discharged home with instructions to follow up with her allergist and GI specialist, continue oral symptom management, and restart chronic medications as advised by her providers.
